present.explain: A Russian verb's ending says who does it: я пью (I drink), ты пьёшь (you drink), он пьёт (he drinks); я читаю, ты читаешь, она читает; я иду, ты идёшь, мы идём, вы идёте. Learn each verb's forms as you meet them: пить and идти change more than their ending.
present.why: English changes its verb only for he and she; Russian changes it for everyone, so [[пью]] already says I drink. The same form says I drink and I'm drinking: Russian has no -ing.

examples.text: Мы идём домой, а он читает.
examples.means: We're going home, and he's reading.
examples.literal: We go home, and he reads.

contrasts.says: English adds -s only for he and she, and says I'm drinking with -ing; Russian has one form for both, with an ending for each person.
After хочу or могу, the next verb takes no ending: Я хочу пить.

mistakes.why: With я, it's пью.
With ты, it's читаешь.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

gender.explain: Every Russian noun is a он word, a она word or an оно word, and the words with it match: один чай, одна машина; мой телефон, моя машина. Most nouns ending in a consonant are он words (телефон, ключ, дом), most ending in -а are она words (сумка, машина, мама), and most ending in -о are оно words (молоко). кофе is a он word though it ends in -е.
gender.why: English has he, she and it for people and for what you point back to; Russian sorts every noun this way, so a phone is он: Где телефон? [[Он]] здесь. Learn which with the word; the ending usually tells you.

examples.means: My coffee is on the table.

contrasts.says: English calls a thing it; Russian calls a телефон он and a сумка она, as it would a man and a woman.
мой and твой follow the noun's gender: мой ключ, моя сумка.

mistakes.why: телефон is a он word: мой.
чай is a он word: один.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

no-be.explain: In the present, Russian says no am, is or are: Я дома (I'm at home), Телефон на столе (the phone is on the table), Где ключ? (where's the key?). The words just stand side by side.
no-be.why: English needs a verb in every sentence; Russian leaves to be out in the present, as an English headline does (Phone on table).

contrasts.says: English can't leave is out (The phone on the table isn't a sentence); Russian always does in the present.
Это alone says this is: Это мой ключ (this my key).

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

question.explain: A yes/no question keeps a statement's order; only the voice rises on the word asked about (the ? when written): Машина здесь. (the car's here) → Машина здесь? (is the car here?). A question word (где, что, чей) most often comes first: Где машина? Что ты читаешь?
question.why: English turns words around or adds do (Do you drink coffee?); Russian changes nothing but the voice: Ты пьёшь кофе? There's no do in Russian at all.

contrasts.says: English moves is or adds do (Is the car here? Do you read?); Russian keeps the order and lets the voice ask.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

accusative.explain: What you drink, read or hold takes the accusative. For она words ending in -а, the -а becomes -у: вода → Я пью воду, книга → Я читаю книгу, газета → Он читает газету. он and оно words stay as they are: Я пью чай, Я пью молоко.
accusative.why: English shows who does what by order alone; Russian also marks it on the word, so [[воду]] is water as what's drunk, wherever it stands.

contrasts.says: English never changes water for what you drink; Russian does: вода, воду.
Where something is takes -е instead: в машине, на столе.

mistakes.why: What you drink: воду.
What he reads: книгу.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

prepositional.explain: After в (in) and на (on, at), where something is takes the prepositional, mostly ending in -е: стол → на столе, сумка → в сумке, машина → в машине, работа → на работе.
prepositional.why: English says where with in and on alone; Russian says it twice, with the little word and with the ending, so [[столе]] after на is the table as a place.

examples.means: The key is on the table.
The phone is in the bag.

contrasts.says: English's on and in change nothing after them; Russian's change the word.
дома (at home) and домой (home, going there) say it without в or на.

mistakes.why: After в, where it is: сумке.
After на, where she is: работе.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

possessive.explain: мой (my) and твой (your) match their noun as an adjective does: мой телефон, моя сумка; твой ключ, твоя машина. твой is for someone you say ты to.
possessive.why: English's my never changes; Russian's follows the noun's gender, so [[моя]] tells you сумка is a она word.

examples.means: Your bag is on the table.

contrasts.says: The noun's gender decides: мой for он words, моя for она words.
English has one my; Russian has мой and моя, and more forms you'll meet.

mistakes.why: ключ is a он word: мой.
сумка is a она word: твоя.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

short-adjective.explain: A few adjectives have a short form for how someone is, and it says the gender: готов (a man), готова (a woman), готовы (more than one, or вы). Я готов. Она готова. Мы готовы.
short-adjective.why: English's ready is the same for everyone; Russian's says who it's about, so a woman says Я [[готова]] and a man Я готов.

contrasts.says: English says ready for anyone; Russian's form says a man, a woman or more than one.
With вы, even to one person, it's готовы.

mistakes.why: With мы: готовы.
With она: готова.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

direction.explain: Being somewhere and going there are different words: дома is at home, домой is home as where you go: Я дома (I'm at home), Я иду домой (I'm going home).
direction.why: English uses home for both; Russian asks where at or where to. A verb of going takes [[домой]]; being, drinking or reading there takes дома.

contrasts.says: English's home is both; Russian's дома is where you are and домой where you go.
идти (to go) takes домой: Я иду домой.

mistakes.why: Where you are: дома.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

ne.explain: не goes right before the word it denies, most often the verb: Я не пью кофе (I don't drink coffee), Я не могу помочь (I can't help). Russian has no do: не alone says don't.
ne.why: English needs do to say not (I don't drink); Russian puts [[не]] in front of the verb and changes nothing else.

contrasts.says: English adds do or does (I don't, she doesn't); Russian never does.
With nothing to have, нет takes есть's place: У меня нет работы.

mistakes.why: Before a verb it's не; нет is no.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

infinitive.explain: After хочу (I want), могу (I can) and давай (let's), the next verb stays in its dictionary form: Я хочу пить, Я могу помочь, Давай пить чай.
infinitive.why: English says to after want (I want to drink) and nothing after can; Russian needs neither: the dictionary form, like [[пить]], does it.

contrasts.says: Only the first verb takes the ending: Я хочу пить.
English adds to after want; Russian adds nothing.

mistakes.why: After хочу, the dictionary form: пить.
After могу: помочь.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

have.explain: To say you have something, Russian says it's at you: У меня есть работа (at me is work: I have work), У тебя есть машина? (do you have a car?). With none, нет takes есть's place, and the thing takes the genitive: У меня нет работы.
have.why: English's have is a verb of its own; Russian builds it from у (at) and меня (me), so У меня есть is I have, and the thing you have is the sentence's subject.

examples.means: I still have work to do.

contrasts.says: English's have is a verb; Russian says the thing is at you.
With нет, the thing takes the genitive: работа becomes работы.

mistakes.why: What you have stays as it is: работа.
After у, я becomes меня.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

demonstrative.explain: этот (this) matches its noun: этот телефон, эта сумка. это on its own says this is or that's, with no is, and never changes: Это мой ключ, Это сумка мамы.
demonstrative.why: English says this for both; Russian's этот points at a thing and matches it, and это presents one: Это [[машина]] мамы (this is Mom's car).

contrasts.says: After its noun, мой or моя alone says mine: Этот телефон мой.
Это alone says this is.

mistakes.why: сумка is a она word: эта.
телефон is a он word: этот.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

address.explain: ты is for one person you know well; вы is for someone you don't know well, or for more than one, and takes the plural verb form: Ты идёшь домой? to a friend, Вы идёте домой? to a stranger or to two friends.
address.why: English has one you; Russian chooses, and the verb's ending follows: вы [[идёте]].

contrasts.says: English's you is one word for everyone; Russian's says how well you know them, or that there's more than one.
With вы, even to one person, it's готовы.

mistakes.why: With вы: идёте.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.
